content:
What are some examples of theorems that were proved formally before they were proved on a napkin/notepad/published PDF?

This is partially a self-serving question because that is what happened with the main result in my recent paper on deontic logic (https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17703, to appear in Studia Logica).
I was wondering what the models of some theory were, and could only think of three. So I ambitiously wrote out in Lean the statement that these three were the only ones, and started plugging away. Mostly expecting to find, this way, that were other models. To my surprise, a couple of weeks later it turned out that yes, there are only those 3. To this day I can't really say that I "understand" the proof in the same way that we used to understand proofs.

Some small and insignificant examples are in my Ph.D. thesis:
https://madvorak.github.io/2026_Dvorak_Martin_Thesis_improved.pdf
Section 6.2 briefly lists results that were new theorems to the best of my knowledge.

The project on implications between magma equations
https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/
is kinda a large database of such problems.
The answer to your question largely depends on what you consider to be a new result. If the theorem was never stated before but it was solvable using preëxisting techniques, is it a new result?
In a slightly opposite direction, I disproved the result discussed in https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.08139 formally before elsewhere.

For a while I have been annoying my coauthors in https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05801 with not fully understanding/believing/accepting our proofs until I managed to reproduce them in Lean, as now described in the appendix. So it wasn't really "Lean first" but more like "Napkin first by person A, then Lean by B, then PDF by A".

Not sure if it counts, but in my community (programming languages), there are many papers whether all theorems are only proved directly in a proof assistant without any napkin / paper proof. This certainly applies to basically all of my papers.
(I did a proof on paper once for one paper. It was very annoying and I don't plan to do so again soon.)

I'm not sure whether this is the kind of example you're looking for in that it's a proof simplification rather than an independent theorem (though the boundary there seems blurry) but an example of formalization-first simplification is Johan Commelin's simplification of an argument of Scholze as part of the Liquid Tensor Experiment. https://math.commelin.net/files/LTE.pdf has some details
I guess I don't know whether Johan wrote it on paper first :) maybe he did.

In this paper on Diophantine equations that I coauthored (w/ @Marco David) we only managed to get the precise bound η\etaη in Theorem A through formalisation (in Isabelle). The main ideas of the construction were known before though. We had to translate a few proofs from Isabelle to English/LaTeX in the end.

Martin Dvořák said:

The answer to your question largely depends on what you consider to be a new result. If the theorem was never stated before but it was solvable using preëxisting techniques, is it a new result?

Maybe not... although we can make a joking distinction:
preexisting (= already exists) => still a new result
preëxisting (= has existed for centuries) => probably not really a new result
CGT#Surreal.birthday_toGame was proven by @Aaron Liu before either of us really understood the proof, to our knowledge this result doesn't appear in the literature.

I think the proof of the fifth busy beaver number counts, as that statement was proved in Rocq before any complete proof had been written down in any other medium. https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/BB(5)

Violeta Hernández said:

CGT#Surreal.birthday_toGame was proven by Aaron Liu before either of us really understood the proof, to our knowledge this result doesn't appear in the literature.

I thought I saw something like this in metamath and thought that this was done before, but he cites your result. :rolling_on_the_floor_laughing:
